title: Clean Execution: How to Cut and Avoid Being Hit
subtitle: Petr Vasiliev’s longsword seminar in Istanbul on linking every cut to blade control, managing distance after a hit, and building continuous defensive movement.
source_name: Workshop Clean execution  How to cut and avoid being hit
note: The seminar is conducted primarily in English. The summary, semantic structure, study materials, and full transcript are presented in English.
overview_theses: A clean exchange does not end when the cut lands: the fencer must immediately control the opponent’s blade and leave under cover.
The central training rule is to move from the opponent’s body to the blade and from the blade back to the body, without a break in attention or momentum.
The Endless Battle drill joins familiar cuts, parries, guard changes, and retreats into continuous movement until those transitions become automatic.
The body works like a rubber band: an attack extends the structure, while the following parry and recovery use the natural tendency to contract.
An intentional parry begins before the expected afterblow is fully visible, because the distance after a successful hit is often too short for a purely reactive defense.
Distance is part of the defensive action: a cross-step or deeper retreat can force the opponent to begin a new attack instead of finishing the current one.
The same principle applies after counterattacks, simple attacks, compound attacks, and a flèche: choose the closest available defense, then recover under control.
Drills should train adaptable motor solutions rather than permanently tying one cut to one fixed step or one fixed partner signal.

chapters.title: Warm-Up and Workshop Setup
chapters.summary: The group organizes the space, introduces the instructor, and warms the joints and legs for the rotational and retreating movements used later.
chapters.anchor: We just handle it like this No, not at all Okay, guys, let's line up in front of me Wait
theses: The warm-up uses jumping, lateral movement over the sword, shoulder mobility, and torso rotation.
Foot placement during rotation is already treated as technical preparation rather than generic exercise.

chapters.title: Clean Execution Means Surviving the Exchange
chapters.summary: The seminar’s problem is defined: a fencer often recognizes the attack and the final recovery but lacks a practiced connection between the two.
chapters.anchor: Topic of our workshop is clean execution with a cut.
theses: Landing the first hit is not enough if attention disappears before the opponent’s response.
Reliable defense requires connecting familiar positions into one continuous chain rather than treating them as isolated snapshots.

chapters.title: The First Endless Battle Sequence
chapters.summary: The first sequence links a stationary countercut, fourth parry, cross-step retreat, guard change, and the mirrored action from the other side.
chapters.anchor: Our exercise, I call it endless battle because I watch too much anime.
theses: A dritto fendente from Posta di Donna flows directly into the closest fourth parry.
The cross-step creates distance while the parry closes the line; a short following step changes the guard without presenting an exposed transition.
The mirrored sequence uses the opposite cut and third parry so the drill can repeat continuously.

chapters.title: Body Mechanics Before Sword Mechanics
chapters.summary: The instructor reframes the sword as a tool moved by the whole body and introduces the rubber-band model of extension and contraction.
chapters.anchor: We really like swords.
theses: Knowing named guards is less useful without posture, coordination, and mobile footwork.
The cut stretches the body; the retreating parry contracts it into another stable position.
Every end position should remain usable for another extension or a further retreat.

chapters.title: Turning the Sequence into a Partner Drill
chapters.summary: A partner supplies a deliberate opening, receives the counterattack, gives an afterblow, and then resets distance so the sequence can continue.
chapters.anchor: Again, my friends, come here, please.
theses: The assistant’s exaggerated preparation creates a readable tempo for the counterattack.
The student answers the afterblow with a retreating parry instead of mentally ending the exchange after the first touch.
Partners change roles at the end of each pass so both sides practice the sequence.

chapters.title: Why an Artificial Drill Builds a Real Skill
chapters.summary: The instructor explains why a repetitive, noncompetitive drill is useful even though its rhythm does not resemble free fencing.
chapters.anchor: modification it's simple we just increase tempo uh when i say so uh we need to discuss why do we need
theses: Knowledge becomes usable only after enough repetitions create a movement habit.
The drill provides many safe repetitions with high activity and little time lost between actions.
Its tactical core is the repeated transition from body to blade and from blade to body.

chapters.title: Tempo, Acceleration, and the Assistant’s Role
chapters.summary: Partners start at a controllable pace and accelerate while the assistant preserves the student’s rhythm instead of turning the exercise into a bout.
chapters.anchor: Okay, guys, wait a second.
theses: The assistant must match the student’s pace without overrunning it or leaving dead time.
Simple, readable cues matter more than realistic fencing posture inside this stage of the drill.
Speed increases only while the sequence remains connected and technically stable.

chapters.title: Why the Drill Is an Endless Loop
chapters.summary: The continuous sequence alternates shoulders, cuts, parries, and retreats until conscious technical commentary gives way to sustained rhythm.
chapters.anchor: Now, I think you get the idea why it's called endless battle.
theses: The loop is intentionally abstract and designed to prevent a pause after each successful action.
Both sides of the body are trained so the student can cut and parry from either shoulder.

chapters.title: The Second Endless Battle Sequence
chapters.summary: The second sequence starts from a closed line, attacks the opposite opening, and uses the matching retreating parry before the next guard change.
chapters.anchor: This is endless battle second sequence.
theses: The assistant closes the shortest line instead of offering the same opening as before.
The student strikes from the opposite side and moves in the direction that supports the following parry.
The two sequences provide interchangeable building blocks rather than a single memorized choreography.

chapters.title: Why the Parry Must Be Intentional
chapters.summary: The instructor shows why being merely faster is unreliable and why defense should already be forming as the hit lands.
chapters.anchor: Here are a few tricks.
theses: At hitting distance, the opponent’s counteraction or afterblow may already be halfway complete.
Waiting to see the full response leaves too little time for perception, decision, and arm movement.
The closest parry is therefore prepared as part of the attack’s completion.

chapters.title: Diagonal Retreat and a Stable Crossed Position
chapters.summary: When an opponent continues forward, the defender increases distance on a slight diagonal and finishes in a crossed stance that remains stable and adaptable.
chapters.anchor: He's just moving forward.
theses: A diagonal retreat can create more usable space than backing straight into the opponent’s pressure.
The crossed position is acceptable only if the fencer can pause, converse, or choose the next direction without falling out of balance.
From that structure the fencer can close forward or continue withdrawing.

chapters.title: Connect the Pieces Without Breaking Rhythm
chapters.summary: Cuts and parries are familiar pieces; the new skill is joining them so the body continues thinking through movement without empty pauses.
chapters.anchor: I show you different pieces of Lego you already knew.
theses: The training priority is continuity, not maximum speed.
The assistant performs fewer actions than the student and must cue the next repetition early enough to preserve tempo.
A slow connected sequence is more useful than a fast sequence broken by hesitation.

chapters.title: Double Hits, Afterblows, and Pre-Emptive Defense
chapters.summary: The first section closes by explaining that both fencers are already moving, so a clean exchange depends on defending before the response fully develops.
chapters.anchor: What happens
theses: After landing, the fencer is commonly too close to rely on a late reactive parry.
The opponent has limited time before the referee’s stop, which makes the expected continuation more constrained than an attack from neutral distance.
The retreating parry turns that constraint into a repeatable clean-exchange habit.

chapters.title: Distance Questions and Independent Building Blocks
chapters.summary: During a break, the instructor answers questions about whether fixed footwork creates bad habits and argues for separating steps from blade actions.
chapters.anchor: Now, I suggest you to take one minute
theses: A motor task should allow the body to select a step size and direction that fit the actual distance.
Training every cut permanently attached to one step can make adaptation harder at close or long measure.
Changing the assistant’s approach provides different distance problems without abandoning the core sequence.

chapters.title: From Fixed Sequences to Variable Signals
chapters.summary: The drill is generalized: once the building blocks are familiar, the assistant may offer different openings and the student chooses the matching cut and parry.
chapters.anchor: So, my friends, we did a fancy exercise.
theses: The fixed sequence can serve as a warm-up or short recurring practice.
After several weeks of regular repetition, concrete signals can be varied without losing the body-to-blade principle.
The technical foundation is now transferred into recognizable fighting situations.

chapters.title: Counterattack from the Central Guard
chapters.summary: Starting from Posta Breve, the student counterattacks an overprepared entry and immediately closes the line of the expected continuation.
chapters.anchor: But we need to move to the fighting situations.
theses: The partner shows a credible attacking line rather than simply waiting to be hit.
The counterattack does not finish with the hands withdrawn; the blade continues into a protective position.
The same solution is practiced against actions from both sides.

chapters.title: Coordinating the Counterattack with the Retreat
chapters.summary: Arm and leg timing is divided into two tempos: counterattack as the rear leg extends, then parry as the lead leg completes the retreat.
chapters.anchor: Let's go to the details.
theses: The counterattack begins from place while the body is already starting to leave distance.
The second retreating step supports the parry and gives the opponent less access to a follow-up.
The attacker’s cue should represent an overcommitted or compound preparation, not a direct attack that would tactically call for a simple parry.

chapters.title: Make the Training Cue Look Like an Attack
chapters.summary: The assistant replaces a passive signal with a slow but committed action so the student must find the counterattack and defense inside realistic forward pressure.
chapters.anchor: Wait one second, please.
theses: A cooperative cue should remain readable without teaching the student to wait for an artificial pause.
Practicing against a slow continuous attack exposes errors that would be impossible to repair at full speed.
The student is responsible for finding the timing rather than receiving a perfectly timed target.

chapters.title: Parrying Either Side of the Afterblow
chapters.summary: The assistant may continue on the original line or redirect to the other side, while the student keeps the first defensive position calm and ready to adapt.
chapters.anchor: The difficulty.
theses: The initial parry closes the shortest continuation without becoming a rigid commitment.
A calm guard position preserves options for a second parry, another hit, or renewed movement.
Variation in the assistant’s follow-up prevents the drill from becoming a single anticipated answer.

chapters.title: Full Extension, Reach, and Joint Safety
chapters.summary: The counterattack is refined so the arms reach fully at the hit, the distance is adjusted with the feet, and the retreat absorbs the remaining momentum safely.
chapters.anchor: Technique.
theses: Stopping a high-speed extension halfway and reversing it repeatedly can overload the elbow.
The blade should reach with the pointward part while the legs create enough space for the following parry.
The sword’s rebound is redirected into defense instead of being arrested and restarted.

chapters.title: Troubleshooting Distance and Rebound
chapters.summary: When the extended counterattack makes the next defense fail, the instructor diagnoses either insufficient retreat or wasted blade momentum.
chapters.anchor: he lands a strike and uh he break through your defense uh there is two possible problems first
theses: A deeper back step can make the opponent start a new attack instead of carrying the first one through the defense.
The natural ricochet from the opponent’s hands can be caught and thrown toward the expected afterblow.
With correct distance and leverage, even an extended-arm parry can remain structurally sound.

chapters.title: When Another Counterattack Is the Better Answer
chapters.summary: A participant challenges the long retreat, leading to a tactical discussion of when to counterattack again, thrust, beat the blade, or use the trained parry as a backup.
chapters.anchor: I totally understand this.
theses: The drill isolates distance management; it does not claim that retreating is the best answer in every exchange.
A clear, readable compound attack may allow another counterattack or a stopping thrust.
The pre-emptive parry remains valuable when the action is ambiguous or there is not enough time to choose the ideal tactical response.

chapters.title: Applying the Principle After a Simple Attack
chapters.summary: The seminar moves from defensive counterattacks to initiated attacks: strike the opening, observe the opponent’s blade, and continue toward it immediately.
chapters.anchor: Let's go to the next exercise.
theses: The exercise deliberately begins after any earlier beat, engagement, feint, or preparation has already done its work.
The attacker cuts to the hands or head and shapes the finish so only a small adjustment is needed to parry.
The partner supplies an afterblow rather than a passive target.

chapters.title: Extended-Arm Parry and Immediate Continuation
chapters.summary: The attacker practices receiving the afterblow with nearly straight arms so the sword remains close to the opponent and ready to cut or thrust again.
chapters.anchor: Try to parry with your arms fully extended.
theses: A compact parry close to the body remains possible, but the drill emphasizes controlling space farther forward.
If the first attack misses or meets a defense, the extended structure supports an immediate second action.
The attacker retreats only as far as required to make the parry work.

chapters.title: Separate a Simple Attack from a Counterattack
chapters.summary: The instructor corrects students who keep counterattacking and redesigns the cue so the student clearly initiates a simple attack before parrying and riposting.
chapters.anchor: But we already do counterattacks.
theses: The assistant begins in a deliberately hittable position and reacts during the student’s forward step.
The sequence is attack, parry, then riposte—not counterattack followed by riposte.
The cue must arrive early enough to create a genuine afterblow without collapsing into an uncontrolled double hit.

chapters.title: Choose the Closest Defense After Any Hit
chapters.summary: Cuts, parries, leading legs, and directions are treated as modular building blocks for selecting the nearest defense at the instant an attack finishes.
chapters.anchor: And let's go for the last exercise.
theses: The rule survives changes in the preceding action: simple attack, compound attack, beat, or feint.
Third, fourth, and sixth parries cover many common needs, but the principle is not limited to those named actions.
The relevant question is where the opponent’s blade is when the hit lands and which defense is closest from that position.

chapters.title: Recovering Safely from a Flèche
chapters.summary: The final drill applies the same rule to a flèche, where forward momentum prevents an immediate stop and makes the likely afterblow especially predictable.
chapters.anchor: We go for the flash.
theses: After the attacking foot lands, the fencer contracts behind the blade instead of remaining fully extended and exposed.
The sword closes the likely line while the feet continue to dissipate forward momentum.
After the parry, the fencer may crowd safely, move laterally, or recover distance according to the situation.

chapters.title: Shrink the Target in the Crucial Moment
chapters.summary: Lowering and contracting the body briefly reduces available targets, reinforces the parry, and creates a protected transition back to normal movement.
chapters.anchor: Maneuvering.
theses: A low posture is not proposed as a permanent fencing stance, but as a short defensive phase.
Bending and moving toward the protection can shorten openings while the body is still too close to disengage freely.
The fencer extends again only after the immediate danger is controlled.

chapters.title: Continue Until the Exchange Is Truly Over
chapters.summary: The seminar closes by restating the body-to-blade cycle, the rubber-band model, and the conditions under which a fencer may finally relax.
chapters.anchor: Until.
theses: After a hit, the fencer continues to the blade instead of turning away or assuming the point has ended the danger.
Only clear physical separation or the referee’s stop makes it safe to discontinue defensive control.
Students are encouraged to remember the felt shape of a successful continuous exchange rather than trying to memorize every sentence or drill detail.

notes.title: The Core Cycle
items: Move from the opponent’s body to the blade after your hit, then from the blade back to the body when the next offensive opportunity appears.
Do not treat the first touch as the end of the exchange. Continue until distance or the referee’s command makes the opponent physically unable to hit you.

notes.title: The Rubber-Band Model
items: A cut extends the body and weapon; the following parry and retreat reuse that momentum by contracting into a stable position.
The objective is not to stop the sword and start a separate defense, but to redirect the existing movement into the closest protective line.

notes.title: How to Use the Endless Battle Drill
items: Begin with fixed sequences and readable cues. Increase speed only after cuts, parries, steps, and guard changes remain continuous.
Later vary the opening, attacking side, and partner pressure so the student selects a response from familiar building blocks instead of replaying choreography.
A suggested recurring dose from the seminar is five to ten minutes, two or three times per week, over several weeks.

notes.title: Distance and Tactical Choice
items: Retreat far enough that the opponent cannot simply finish the current attack through your defense. A diagonal exit may create a more stable and useful position than moving straight back.
The trained parry is a robust backup, not the only tactical answer. When the continuation is clear, another counterattack, a thrust, or a blade beat may be preferable.

items.text: Link a stationary dritto fendente to fourth parry, cross-step retreat, short recovery step, and guard change; repeat the mirrored sequence from the other side.
Use the second sequence: the assistant closes the closest line, the student cuts the opposite opening, retreats into the matching parry, and changes guard.
Perform both sequences slowly without pauses, then increase tempo while preserving a continuous three-action rhythm.
From Posta Breve, counterattack the partner’s overprepared entry and immediately close the expected afterblow line.
Coordinate the counterattack with rear-leg extension, then complete the retreat and parry on the lead leg’s movement.
Replace the static cue with a slow committed attack so the student must find timing and defense within forward pressure.
Let the assistant choose a simple or compound continuation; keep the first guard calm and redirect to either side as needed.
Initiate a simple cut to an offered opening, move directly toward the partner’s afterblow line, and riposte only after the defense is complete.
Repeat with nearly straight arms in the parry so the weapon stays forward and can continue immediately if the first attack fails.
Use an early partner cue to distinguish the initiated attack–parry–riposte sequence from the earlier counterattack drill.
Attack with a flèche, continue the necessary forward steps, contract behind the blade on landing, parry the predictable afterblow, and recover under cover.
